summary: Psalm 4 opens with a speaker asking God for an answer, relief, mercy, and a hearing. The speaker then addresses “sons of men,” warns them away from dishonor and falsehood, calls for stillness, sacrifice, and trust, and ends with gladness and sleep in safety.
whyItMatters: This short psalm shows an early Book I pattern: pressure is brought to God, opponents or doubters are addressed, and trust becomes the closing posture. It also preserves performance signals, including stringed instruments and Selah, without explaining exactly how they were used.

context.author: Many writers and collections; this psalm’s heading says “A Psalm by David,” while the briefing notes that Davidic headings are ancient but debated as authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later adopted by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a David-associated section marked by prayers of distress and confidence; this chapter itself names no specific historical event.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a musical heading, direct address to God, address to others, and a closing statement of trust.

outline.heading: A Plea for an Answer
outline.note: The speaker calls on God, asks for relief from distress, and asks for mercy and a hearing.

outline.heading: A Challenge to the Sons of Men
outline.note: The speaker confronts those who turn glory into dishonor and seek falsehood, then affirms that Yahweh hears the godly one.

outline.heading: Stillness, Sacrifice, and Trust
outline.note: The addressees are told to stand in awe, avoid sin, examine the heart, be still, offer righteous sacrifices, and trust Yahweh.

outline.heading: Good Sought and Given
outline.note: The question “Who will show us any good?” is answered by a request for Yahweh’s face to shine and by gladness greater than harvest abundance.

outline.heading: Peaceful Sleep
outline.note: The psalm ends with the speaker lying down and sleeping because Yahweh alone gives safety.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician; on stringed instruments. A Psalm by David. Answer me when I call, God of my righteousness. Give me relief from my distress. Have mercy on me, and hear my prayer.
keyVerses.why: This verse sets the psalm’s performance frame and its opening posture: urgent prayer for response, relief, mercy, and hearing.

keyVerses.text: But know that Yahweh has set apart for himself him who is godly; Yahweh will hear when I call to him.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the speaker’s confidence after the accusation of dishonor and falsehood.

keyVerses.text: Many say, “Who will show us any good?” Yahweh, let the light of your face shine on us.
keyVerses.why: This gives the chapter’s central contrast between anxious public questioning and the speaker’s appeal to Yahweh’s favor.

keyVerses.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, Yahweh, make me live in safety.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse shows the movement from distress to settled trust.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” so the received text associates the poem with David. The book briefing cautions that Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers differ on how much they establish historically. The voice inside the psalm is an individual speaker calling to God and addressing other people.

questions.question: What does “For the Chief Musician; on stringed instruments” tell us?
questions.answer: It is a performance heading attached to the psalm. It points to musical or liturgical use, but the briefing says the ancient melodies and exact force of several performance terms are lost. The safest claim is that the psalm was transmitted with a musical direction.

questions.question: What is the speaker asking God to do in verse 1?
questions.answer: The speaker asks God to answer, give relief from distress, show mercy, and hear the prayer. The verse does not describe the distress in detail. It gives the pressure and the appeal, not the full backstory.

questions.question: Who are the “sons of men”?
questions.answer: The phrase names the people the speaker addresses in verse 2. They are accused of turning the speaker’s glory into dishonor, loving vanity, and seeking falsehood. The chapter does not identify them more specifically, so it is better not to invent a setting or named group.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after verse 2 and again after verse 4. The book briefing describes it as an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. It signals the poem’s performed shape, but it should not be treated as a fully understood command.

questions.question: Does verse 3 prove that the speaker will get every requested outcome immediately?
questions.answer: Verse 3 says Yahweh has set apart the godly one and will hear when the speaker calls. In this chapter, that confidence supports the speaker’s movement toward peace. It does not give details about timing, method, or every circumstance beyond this psalm.

questions.question: Is “Stand in awe, and don’t sin” a command about fear, anger, worship, or something else?
questions.answer: Readers differ on the exact force of the line, especially because short poetic commands can carry more than one shade of meaning. In this chapter, the command is paired with searching one’s heart on the bed and being still, so the emphasis is on restrained, reflective conduct before God. The verse does not spell out a full ritual or psychological process.

questions.question: What are “the sacrifices of righteousness”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in a call to offer sacrifices and trust Yahweh. The chapter does not define the sacrifices or describe an altar scene. At minimum, the line joins worship practice with righteousness and trust rather than treating sacrifice as an isolated act.

questions.question: Why compare gladness with grain and new wine?
questions.answer: Verse 7 compares the speaker’s gladness with the joy people have when grain and new wine increase. The comparison uses ordinary abundance as a measure of happiness. The speaker says God-given gladness is greater than that increase.

glossary.def: The figure named in the heading connected with the psalm’s musical presentation; the chapter does not explain the role further.
Instruments named in the heading as part of the psalm’s performance direction.
A preserved performance marker appearing in verses 2 and 4; its exact meaning is uncertain.
Something the addressed “sons of men” are said to love in verse 2, paired with seeking falsehood.
Part of the harvest abundance named in verse 7, used as a comparison for gladness.
